_README: Machine-readable record of every per-dataset decision. `verified_by` quotes the evidence. NOTE ON WINSORISING, which applies across the collection: many of these papers run their headline regressions on winsorised copies of the effect and standard error, built inside their own replication code. In nearly every case those copies do not exist in the published file, so the harmonised table carries the RAW columns. armington is the one literature that ships both, and we take raw there too, for one consistent rule. Consequence: our values will not reproduce those papers' published coefficients until you apply the paper's own winsorising.

lags.reason: outcome is the transmission lag (mon_bot, months to the price trough); it has no sampling standard error, so it cannot enter an effect/SE table
lags.verified_by: lags.do keeps horizon==99 and models mon_bot directly; the se/up/low on that row belong to the price-response magnitude, not to the lag

price_puzzle.units: proportional change in the price level
price_puzzle.verified_by: puzzle.do computes t=res/se and prec=1/se on the long form restricted to horizon in {3,6,12,18,36}; the published file is wide, so the M{h}R / SE{h} pairs are reshaped here to reproduce it. Median |t| is 0.75-0.91 across horizons, consistent with the literature's mostly insignificant responses.
price_puzzle.note: puzzle.xls is a HYBRID layout: already long on `horizon` (7 rows per impulse response) while the response columns are WIDE and constant across those 7. Melting the wide columns once per row emitted every estimate 7 times -- what 0.9.0-beta shipped: 7,420 rows of which ~6,345 were exact duplicates, identical in every column INCLUDING horizon, so they were never additional horizons. The file provides SEVEN horizons, not five: the month horizons 3/6/12/18/36 plus the trough (MBR/SEB, horizon code 99) and the peak (MPR/SEP, horizon code 88). puzzle.do line 29 excludes `horizon~=88 & horizon~=99` from its 'all horizons' figure and its headline regressions use the five month horizons, so the paper analyses five -- but this catalogue publishes what the file contains, and the trough and peak responses were being silently discarded. All seven are now emitted from the deduplicated records: 1,415 rows (211/218/218/220/208 for the month horizons, 202 trough, 138 peak). Owner's decision 2026-08-04: list every horizon. Anyone wanting the paper's own sample should filter to the five numeric horizons. HORIZON CODES: months 3/6/12/18/36 are literal; 99 marks the trough and 88 the peak, the source file's own codes. The trough/peak assignment is inferred from lags.do, which keeps horizon==99 and models mon_bot, the months to the price trough. If that is backwards the two labels swap and no value changes. Filter to horizon<=36 for the paper's own sample.

climate.verified_by: climate.do builds prec=1/se_low and runs all FAT-PET and funnel regressions on se_low; se_up appears only in one robustness line

house_prices.verified_by: house.do rescales est to percent and sets SE=(SE_l+SE_u)/2; seraw is populated on only 40 of 1785 rows. Restricting to inlevels==1 (the paper's own main sample) yields exactly 1,555 usable estimates, matching the abstract; the 126 growths==1 rows are a different specification.
house_prices.note: one row per impulse-response horizon, roughly 7 horizons per (idstudy, idirf), so rows within a study are not independent

bma.verified_by: determinants.do runs 'drop if aux==1' then 'drop if horiz!=1'. Applying exactly those two filters yields 1,205 usable estimates, matching the abstract exactly.
bma.note: HORIZONTAL spillovers. Shares the FDI spillovers database with the 'spillovers' project, which takes the vertical subset. The two are complementary, not duplicates.

spillovers.verified_by: Stata_program.do runs 'drop if aux==1' and defines back = (horiz==0 & forw==0) | (horiz==0 & local==1), i.e. the non-horizontal complement
spillovers.note: VERTICAL spillovers (forward and backward). CAUTION: the filtered count is 2,421 while the paper's abstract reports 3,626 estimates, so the published file appears to be a subset of the sample behind the paper. Reconcile before relying on the count.
spillovers.reconciliation_note: The filtered count is 2,421 against the abstract's 3,626. The vertical/horizontal split is applied exactly as the paper's code defines it, so the remaining gap is NOT explained by filtering: the published file appears narrower than the sample behind the paper. Unresolved - treat the count as the file's, not the paper's.

fdi.reason: no per-estimate precision exists: the file has no standard error, t-statistic, weight or inverse-SE column, so SE-based synthesis is impossible
fdi.verified_by: spillovers.R uses e_w (winsorized spillover elasticity) as the response in a Bayesian model averaging regression over moderators; the zip contains only that script and the data. No_of_firms is a log-scaled moderator, not a recoverable N
fdi.note: still fully usable for model averaging over study characteristics, as in the original paper; it is only the effect/SE table it cannot join

reforms.verified_by: reform.do converts lib (a t-statistic, NOT a coefficient) to pcor=lib/sqrt(lib^2+df) with se_pcor=sqrt((1-pcor^2)/df); df=n-k holds exactly on all 456 rows. It then caps lib<12, drops a flagged outlier set defined on the computed correlation ((1/se_pcor)>15 & pcor>0.3 & lib<12) and drops rg==0. Applying all of it gives exactly the 245 short-run coefficients the paper reports.
reforms.note: lib is short-run, lib_cum long-run; the short-run t-statistic is used here

scc.units: US dollars per tonne of carbon
scc.verified_by: scc.do labels stdlow 'Standard error' and runs the funnel-asymmetry regression 'reg scc stdlow'; stdup is an alternative built from the upper CI bound for robustness
scc.note: usable only on the subset where stdlow is present (about 53% of rows); there is no primary-study sample size, perstudy is an estimates-per-study de-clustering weight

forward.units: slope coefficient in the forward premium regression (null of interest is 1, not 0)
forward.verified_by: forward.do runs 'sum beta se' immediately after loading; T and N reproduce ln(Sample_size), so neither is a t-statistic

substitution.reason: same 2,735 estimates as the eis project
substitution.note: Different PAPER (why intertemporal substitution varies across countries) but the same underlying estimates as 'eis', so including both would double count. The substitution file carries 65 columns against eis's 52, including country-level moderators, and remains published in full as its own dataset. Both projects fill the same 18 harmonised moderators, so the choice of which to keep costs nothing; eis is kept as the already-canonical entry.

_DEDUP_RULE: Two projects can publish the same estimates (two papers, one dataset). Keeping both double counts. RULE: keep the project that fills strictly more harmonised moderators; on a tie keep the one whose paper is published; always record the other's DOI in the note so citation stays unambiguous. Both remain published individually under /data/v1/ regardless.

hedge.reason: same 1,019 estimates as the alphas project
hedge.verified_by: effect, se and study_id are element-wise identical across all 1,019 rows; a pairwise scan of the (effect,se) value multiset over all 41 literatures found this as the only remaining duplicate pair
hedge.note: Two papers on one dataset. 'alphas' is kept because it fills 10 harmonised moderators against hedge's 7, and hedge's set is a strict subset, so nothing is lost. CITE the published version for these estimates: Is research on hedge fund performance published selectively? A quantitative survey, Journal of Economic Surveys 2024 (DOI on the hedge dataset entry). The hedge file remains published in full as its own dataset.

trust.reason: same literature as the size project (the size premium); 1,256 of its estimates also appear there
trust.verified_by: The paper's own replication code regresses this effect column: replication.zip:replication_package/R/04_diagnostics.R:78 runs lm(size ~ trust_index), the paper's research regression rather than a FAT-PET, so only the effect column is informative there -- and it is `size`, the same column (as size_unwinsorized) this dataset resolves to. Confirmed by 93_codegrep.py once excluded datasets were brought into its scope, 2026-08-04.
trust.note: INCLUDED from 1.0.0 by the owner's decision (2026-08-04), but only the estimates `size` does not already carry. Of trust's 1,613 rows, 1,329 (82.4%) duplicate pooled `size` rows and are dropped here so nothing is counted twice, leaving the 284 unique to trust that the shipped table carries. This is a deliberate splice of two separately-assembled collections of one literature: trust (2026) is the later collection, size (2019) the earlier and larger one at 1,746 rows. Anyone who wants either collection whole should use its own per-dataset file rather than the pooled table.

remittances.note: The file holds BOTH a long-run (COEF_L/SE_L) and a short-run (COEF_S/SE_S) coefficient per row. Only the LONG-RUN pair enters the harmonised table, because the two are different estimands and pooling them would mix horizons. The short-run pair (48 usable rows) remains in the published per-dataset file for anyone who wants it. APPLIED 1.0.0: the effect is now the partial correlation the paper analyses, PCC = TSTAT_L/sqrt(TSTAT_L^2+DF) with se = sqrt((1-PCC^2)/DF), replacing the raw COEF_L/SE_L which ran over five different dependent variables and were not comparable. n_obs is set to NULL: the column matched by name was a row ordinal -- all 490 values unique, strictly increasing over 1..538, and degrees of freedom exceed it on 38.4% of rows, which is impossible for a sample size. A null is honest; leaving it would silently corrupt MAIVE, which instruments precision with sample size. Both found by the Codex audit, 2026-08-04.
remittances.verified_by: COEF_L/SE_L reproduces TSTAT_L exactly on all 490 usable rows (checked numerically), so the stored pairing is internally correct. remittances.do line 2 shows what the PAPER analyses, and it is not that pair: `gen PCC_L=TSTAT_L/sqrt(TSTAT_L^2+DF)`, with SE_PCC_L=sqrt((1-PCC_L^2)/DF); the headline `mean PCC_L` and `metan PCC_L SE_PCC_L` and the whole BMA section run on PCC_L. The short-run set is an appendix robustness check on 48 observations, not pooled. n_obs=Sample: Sample, NOT Obs. Both exist; Obs was rejected earlier and that rejection was right but incomplete, because it left n_obs empty rather than moving to the correct column. Sample is integral, has no nulls across 538 source rows, and runs 6 to 2,946, which is the plausible range for the micro studies this literature pools.

learning.verified_by: 00_setup.R reads the workbook with no sheet argument, so readxl takes the FIRST sheet, which is 'data'. Our picker chose 'Betthauser', a sheet named after a study. The two are byte-identical on the shared columns today, so no number changes, but that identity is coincidental and the reference is pinned to 'data'. ('data_old' is a stale earlier version and must not be used.) n_obs=n_study: n_study is the study's sample size: 291 rows, no nulls, integral, 275 to 10,884,922 — the wide range is the learning-by-doing literature's panel sizes. It is the only sample-size column in the file, so there is nothing to choose between.

electricity.verified_by: electricity.R line 74 defines the analysis sample as in_M_pool==1 & formula==1 & is.finite(effect_M) & se_source!='imputed_uniform_t', and its own header comment states this is 3,324 of the 4,720 usable-SE corpus. Reproduced exactly. effect_M is the Slutsky-converted Marshallian-equivalent measure the paper analyses; it correlates 0.9998 with the raw effect on this sample.
electricity.note: Price elasticity of electricity demand. The pool spans short-run (median -0.16), intermediate-run (-0.39) and long-run (-0.35) estimates, which the paper analyses SEPARATELY; the short_run / intermediate_run / long_run flags are in the per-dataset file, and you should condition on them rather than pool blind. Income elasticities are a different estimand and are kept in their own columns, not mixed in here.

discrate.note: Only the 539 estimates with a GENUINELY REPORTED standard error are included. The paper's headline FAT-PET instead uses standard_error_comb, which imputes a bootstrapped study-level SE for the other 388; that is its 'robust check' specification we match, not its headline. The choice is deliberate: imputed standard errors would contaminate a benchmark whose purpose is comparing standard-error-based correctors. Use the per-dataset file if you want the imputed variant. Negative discount rates are real, not a sign error: a minority of studies estimate them. pub_year is mapped explicitly to `year` (1979-2017). The column NAMED publication_year in this file is a standardised BMA regressor spanning -2.515..1.359, not a year; find_year's value gate correctly rejects it, and `year` is too ambiguous a name to add to the global pattern without risking a data year elsewhere.
discrate.verified_by: discrate.do line 10 destrings standard_error; lines 204-208 are the paper's own 'PET robust check' using standard_error_win if !missing(standard_error), which reproduces this 539-of-927 subset exactly. Also verified there that sample_size == ln(nobs) for all 927 rows, which is why n_obs maps to nobs and not to sample_size.

incentives.verified_by: incentives.do lines 57-60 drop include==2 and bma==0 to form the baseline sample. The mean partial correlation on that sample is 0.05118, matching the paper's stated 0.051 exactly (1,252 estimates). The previous mapping used cohens_d unfiltered, which is the paper's ROBUSTNESS dataset, not its baseline: 'For robustness checks, we consider two additional datasets. First, instead of correlations we look at Cohen's d.'
incentives.note: Baseline is the partial correlation. Cohen's d and its standard error remain in the per-dataset file for anyone wanting the robustness variant.

eis.verified_by: eis.do line 106 restricts DESCRIPTIVE statistics to abs(eis)<10; the regressions use all 2,735 rows with prec=1/se.
eis.note: All 2,735 estimates are included. The extremes (to +/-100,000, with standard errors that scale with them) are REAL weak-instrument Euler-equation estimates, not missing-value sentinels, and the paper keeps them, relying on precision weighting to down-weight them. If you compute a raw MEAN, apply abs(eis)<10 as the paper does for its descriptives: that gives 0.49, matching its reported 0.5, where the unrestricted mean is 41.7. The median is barely affected either way.

compute.factor_col: Multiplicator to obtain estimates in points (number)

activism.verified_by: activism.R sets data$elasticity <- data$Estim_adj and data$se_all <- data$Se_adj, having first deleted the raw Estimate and se columns; the second header row of the published workbook marks them 'Delete' for the same reason. Estim_adj = Estimate*100*Multiplicator, and the Multiplicator takes only the values 0.01 and 1, i.e. the raw column MIXES percent and decimal scales across studies. Reconstructing it gives a median of 0.489, matching the paper's Estim_adj. n_obs=TotalObs: TotalObs is the observation count the paper's own replication code treats as N. Integral, 2 to 11,884, and null on exactly one source row — row 0, which also lacks ArticleNo and does not carry a usable (effect, se) pair, so it is outside the harmonised sample.
activism.note: The analysis workbook (data_v14.xlsx) that holds Estim_adj and Se_adj directly was never published, so the comparable estimate is reconstructed from the two columns that were. The paper recovers standard errors from p-values where Se_adj is missing; that step needs the unpublished file, so here the standard error is derived from the reported t-statistic instead and rows without one are dropped. Pooling the RAW Estimate column would silently mix two scales.

gasoline.verified_by: init.do generates se as abs(e/tstat), which is reproduced here. gas_income_revision.dta's 'e' equals mra-data.dta's Ystat exactly (n=701, mean 0.6589), matching the abstract's long-run figure.
gasoline.note: LONG-RUN estimates only. The published gas_income_revision.dta is the long-run subsample; the paper's headline is both horizons (short-run mean 0.28, long-run 0.66). The 845 SHORT-RUN estimates are in mra-data.dta, inside the same gasoline/data.zip, as Ysr with t-statistic tYsr. They are not yet in the harmonised table. 90 rows carry n_obs <= 1, which is not a usable sample size -- almost certainly a missing-value code in the source rather than a real count. They are left as they are, but anything using sample size as a precision instrument (MAIVE above all) should drop them first. Flagged on every run by 95_columns. Found 2026-08-04.

frisch.note: Extensive-margin estimates only; the intensive margin is a separate file (data_intensive.xlsx). 532 of 723 rows have a usable standard error. The paper does not drop the rest, it imputes a per-study bootstrapped standard error, which cannot be reproduced without the bootstrap inputs, so they are excluded here rather than filled.
frisch.verified_by: frisch.do: 'gen tstat = frisch/se' and 'winsor2 frisch se, cuts(5 95)' confirm frisch/se as the analysis columns. 532 of 723 rows have a usable standard error (538 non-missing, less 6 zeros). The paper imputes the remainder from a per-study bootstrap rather than dropping them; that input was not published, so they are excluded here rather than filled.

inflation.note: Uses the paper's WINSORISED estimate column (Estimate_win): 45 rows sit exactly at the lower bound -3.85 and 42 at the upper bound 6.0. That is what the paper analyses, but it departs from this collection's usual raw-tails policy and the clumps at the bounds will be visible in any funnel plot.
inflation.verified_by: The paper's own replication code regresses exactly this pair at replication.zip:replication_package_FIXED/stata/Inflation_v34.do:391. Found mechanically by 93_codegrep.py, which reads each paper's code and reads off the two variables of its headline meta-analysis regression.

class.note: Two of 2,819 rows carry a partial correlation outside [-1,1] (1.372 and 1.116), taken straight from the source pcc column. They are almost certainly coding errors in the original file. Kept rather than silently dropped, so the mirror stays faithful to what was published — filter on abs(effect)<=1 if you need a strictly valid correlation. UPSTREAM DATA ERROR, documented rather than silently passed: class.xlsx itself carries two partial correlations outside [-1,1] -- pcc = 1.371675 and 1.116313, sitting beside effect/se_effect of 7.24/1.5671 and 0.967742/0.430108. A correlation cannot leave [-1,1], so these are errors in the authors' own pcc column, not in the conversion; 90_roundtrip confirms both values occur verbatim in the source. A further 73 rows sit exactly at -1 or +1 with positive standard errors, which is also not a coherent PCC/SE pair; 70 of those come from one study. Their combined precision weight is about 1e-6 of the literature's total, so they barely move an inverse-variance estimate, but they are invalid input to any correlation transform. Retained because the table's contract is faithful reproduction, and flagged on every run by 94_sanity. Found 2026-08-04.
class.verified_by: The paper's own replication code regresses pcc_w/se_pcc_w @ class.do:737 -- a winsorised copy of this pair, built inside the script from the raw columns. The published file carries only the raw columns, so they are what the harmonised table can offer. Found mechanically by 93_codegrep.py.

dst.verified_by: dst.do labels ESTIMATE 'Estimate of the DST impact (in %)' and runs 'ivreg2 ESTIMATE SE, cluster(...)' as its main FAT-PET regression. 101 of 162 rows have ESTIMATE, SE, TSTAT and PRECISION jointly non-null; the other 61 have all four blank, so the loss is a genuinely unreported standard error, not a column choice.

excess_sensitivity.verified_by: excess.do lines 14-15: 'gen prec=1/se' and 'gen tstat=excess/se', used through the funnel-asymmetry regressions (e.g. 'ivreg2 excess se if micro==1'). All 3,127 rows carry both. The separate mpc/mpc_se pair is a different estimand and is excluded by the paper's own BMA export.

habits.verified_by: habit.do applies 'drop if missing(se)' and winsorises the standard error only, with no trimming of habit itself: 606 rows less 9 missing se = 597, matching the abstract's '597 estimates from 81 published studies'. 125 of 597 fall outside the theoretical [0,1] range; the paper neither trims nor remarks on it, and this is known behaviour for GMM/DSGE habit estimates.

students.verified_by: students.do lines 14-16: 'drop if idstudy>69', then drop if missing(pcc) or missing(se_pcc). Applying all three gives exactly 861 estimates from 69 studies, matching the paper. Without the idstudy filter the file yields 872, which is what was published before and was recorded as an unexplained surplus. It was not unexplained; the filter was missed.
students.note: The published file carries 892 rows, 31 of which the paper's own code excludes.

water.verified_by: water.do line 90 runs the paper's FAT-PET on exactly this pair: `ivreg2 incomeelasticity standarderror, cluster(studyid)`; line 32 `sum incomeelasticity, detail`. The .do header names the paper: INCOME ELASTICITY OF WATER DEMAND. No winsorising or row-dropping is applied to the main regressions (winsor2 is installed at line 10 but never invoked); the only `if` conditions are descriptive subsample splits and one graph-only restriction at line 77. All 307 rows are the analysis sample.
water.note: This is the INCOME elasticity of water demand, not the price elasticity, so the stored values are positive by expectation and are NOT sign-flipped or absolute-valued. `standarderrorovb` is a derived interaction regressor (standarderror x ovb), not a second standard-error column.

risk.verified_by: rra.do (inside risk.zip) lines 104-110 treat rra/se as the pair: `replace se=0.0001 if se==0`, `gen prec = 1/se`, `replace tstat = rra/se if tstat == .`; every downstream meta-analysis traces to it (funnel plot line 192, PET/PEESE lines 211-337, p-uniform* line 705 `keep idstudy rra_win se_win`). BMACode.R line 61 corroborates. risk.dta carries no alternative effect column across its 61 columns, so there is no rejected candidate.
risk.note: The published risk.dta is ALREADY restricted to econometrically estimated RRA: rra.do line 90 `drop if estimated==0` (dropping calibrated values) and line 92 `drop estimated`, which is why the column is absent from the shipped file. The paper's headline regressions then use rra_win/se_win, winsorised at the 10th/90th percentiles by `winsor2 rra se, suffix(_win) cuts(10 90)` at line 135 -- those columns are GENERATED in code and do not exist in risk.dta, so the raw pair is the only thing the source offers.

sigma.verified_by: sigma.do line 28 `gen tstat = sigma/se` establishes the pair; line 202 runs the headline FAT-PET `ivreg2 sigma_win5 se_win5, cluster (idstudy idcountry)` on winsorised versions built at line 83 by `winsor2 sigma se invsqrtnobs, suffix(_win5) cuts(5 95)`. The paper states it winsorises at the 5% level. sigma.dta contains sigma and se but NOT sigma_win5/se_win5, so the raw pair is the only thing the source offers.
sigma.note: The effect is sigma itself, the elasticity of substitution -- not its inverse and not 1-sigma. Primary studies that estimated a transformation (1/sigma, 1-sigma, (1-sigma)/sigma, rho) were converted back to sigma units before the file was written; formula_code records which transformation the primary study used. About 4% of values are negative and are retained, so sigma is not truncated at zero.

beauty.verified_by: beauty.do line 390 runs the headline FAT-PET `ivreg2 premium_w se_premium_w, cluster(study_id)`, where premium_w/se_premium_w are winsorised copies built at line 69 by `foreach v in premium se_premium premium_sd se_premium_sd { winsor2 `v', suffix(_w) cuts(1 99) }`. The site's beauty.xlsx contains premium and se_premium but NOT premium_w/se_premium_w, so the raw pair is the only thing the source offers.
beauty.note: The effect is the percentage increase in earnings or productivity per one-standard-deviation increase in rated beauty, in percentage points (8.91 means 8.91%). Beauty-PENALTY rows are pooled with premiums at their original sign in the main analysis; only a robustness variable flips them. excluded.xlsx is a PRISMA study-level screen -- those studies never entered beauty.xlsx, so it is not a row filter on this file.

armington.verified_by: armington.do lines 94-96 run the headline FAT-PET on the WINSORISED pair: `ivreg2 armel_w se_w, cluster(idstudy idcountry)`. The paper's equation (1) is sigma_ij = sigma_0 + delta*SE(sigma_ij) + mu_ij, and it states it winsorises at the 2.5% level (mean 1.53 -> 1.45, which armel/armel_w reproduce: 1.531 -> 1.454).
armington.note: DELIBERATE CHOICE, and the one literature where it is a choice: armington.xlsx stores BOTH the raw pair (armel/se) and the winsorised pair (armel_w/se_w), and they differ on 176 of 3,524 rows (armel spans -56.19..78.60, armel_w -0.996..8.505). The harmonised table stores the RAW pair, for consistency with every other literature here -- in sigma, beauty and risk the winsorised columns are generated inside the paper's code and are simply not available in the source, so raw is the only option there. Storing raw everywhere keeps one rule across the table and lets a user winsorise themselves; it does mean our values will NOT reproduce this paper's published coefficients until you apply the 2.5% winsorising yourself. Long-run and short-run elasticities share the column and are separated only by the srun flag; do not pool them without it. tstats_w/invse_w serve an alternative t-based specification and are not the primary pair. CAVEAT ON THAT ADVICE: the note above says not to pool short-run with long-run without the `srun` flag, but `srun` is NOT among the columns the harmonised table carries, so a user of the pooled file cannot follow it. Short-run (556 estimates, mean 0.88) and long-run (2,968, mean 1.65) are therefore indistinguishable there; use the per-dataset armington file, which keeps every original column. Carrying run-length into the pooled schema is staged for 1.0.0. Found by the Fable audit, 2026-08-04.

skill.verified_by: skill.do:174 regresses tstat_coefficient_w on precision_coefficient_w, the WLS form of FAT-PET. Regressing t on precision is algebraically the same test as regressing the effect on its standard error, so it confirms rather than contradicts elasticity/se.

migrant.verified_by: The paper's replication is in R, not Stata: run_replication_package.R:1002 runs stats::lm(elasticity ~ se, data = master, weights = se_weight) and clusters on idstudy -- the FAT-PET on exactly this pair. Found by 93_codegrep.py once R patterns were added; a Stata-only scan had reported this literature as having no regression at all.

gasoline_price.verified_by: No replication code ships with this dataset, so it was verified against the PAPER'S OWN PUBLISHED RESULTS instead, which validates the whole chain end to end rather than just the column names. The abstract of gas_price.pdf states that after correction the average long-run elasticity reaches -0.31 and the short-run -0.09, and that the published averages are 'exaggerated twofold'. Computing from the shipped e/se and the longr flag: long-run n=92, mean -0.691; short-run n=110, mean -0.227; 92+110=202, the full file. Those means are 2.2x and 2.5x the paper's corrected values, reproducing the twofold exaggeration it reports. FAT is -3.57 and -2.89, confirming the strong publication selection the paper is about, and long-run exceeds short-run in magnitude as it states.
